title: Nepal Floods: Teacher's Quick Thinking Saved 1,643 Students as School Was Swept Away
excerpt: Rajendra Dawadi, the 47-year-old headmaster of Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School, evacuated 1,643 children in minutes after receiving a warning call about the glacier-triggered flash flood that has killed over 750 people.
body:
• Headmaster Rajendra Dawadi evacuated 1,643 students from Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School minutes before the building was destroyed by flash floods on August 26
  • The flash flood was triggered by a massive glacier collapse from Langtang Lirung peak, sending a wall of water up to nine metres high downstream at 50 mph
  • Two school staff members — teacher Santos Pariyar and janitor Sultan Lama — were killed in the disaster
  • Nepal's death toll has risen above 750, with over 2,400 missing and more than 10,000 left homeless

At 9:20 on the morning of August 26, Rajendra Dawadi received a phone call that would define the next few minutes of his life — and save 1,643 others. His friend in Betrawati, five miles upstream in Nepal's Trishuli Valley, was frantic. "He said the village was gone: taken by the river," Dawadi recalled. "He told me to run."

Dawadi, the 47-year-old headmaster of Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in Nuwakot district, did not run. He stayed.

Minutes to Evacuate

At the time of the call, 900 students were already inside the three-storey school building for the early shift. Another 700 were en route on foot and by bus, wearing their sky-blue uniforms. The school sat 60 metres above the riverbed — a height no flood in living memory had ever reached.

Dawadi took a moment to assess the threat. Then a parent rushed in to warn that the water was rising rapidly. He rang the school bell and ordered teachers to evacuate the classrooms.

He remembered the buses. Each carried 80 children. He reached all the drivers except one and told them to turn back. Then he spotted the final bus crossing the bridge. "By now, the water was in the school grounds — it was so fast — so I told him to turn around," Dawadi said. "It got to the other side just as the bridge collapsed."

"The children were terrified, but their fear gave them the energy to run up the hill."

— Rajendra Dawadi, headmaster, Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School

One girl suffered a panic attack and was put on the back of a motorbike. The rest fled uphill on foot, with Dawadi following behind. They took shelter beneath a bodhi tree as the floodwaters engulfed and destroyed the school's three-storey buildings below them.

Two Lives Lost

Dawadi's quick thinking saved 1,643 children and nearly all the school's staff. But two did not make it. Santos Pariyar, 32, a newly appointed social history teacher, had come in early to teach extra classes and had returned to his rented room beside the river to cook breakfast when the flood struck. Sultan Lama, the school janitor, handed Dawadi the keys and went back to close the doors. The river took both of them.

Locals have called Dawadi a hero. He is not convinced. "What else could I do?" he said, surveying the muddy ruins where the school once stood.

Scale of the Catastrophe

The flash flood was triggered when a massive chunk of ice and rock — estimated at nearly 50 acres — snapped off the north face of Langtang Lirung peak and plunged 1,200 metres into the gorge of the Lhende Khola river near the Tibet border. Geomorphologist Daniel Shugar of the University of Calgary estimated the impact was so violent that seismologists initially mistook it for an earthquake.

The resulting wall of water, mud, and debris rose nine metres high and surged downstream at up to 50 mph. At bends in the river, the wave sloshed up to heights of 70 metres, tearing houses from foundations and scouring hillsides bare. Eight major settlements, 25 miles of road, and 365 bridges have been destroyed.

Nepal's death toll stood at 752 by Sunday, with 16 killed in Tibet. More than 2,400 people remained missing in Nepal, including 33 British tourists. Over 3,700 people have been rescued. More than 10,000 are homeless and 50,000 are without electricity, water, and connectivity. The loss of 14 hydropower plants removed eight per cent of Nepal's grid capacity.

A Region Familiar with Tragedy

The Trishuli Valley is no stranger to catastrophe. In April 2015, a 7.8-magnitude earthquake killed nearly 9,000 people across South Asia and triggered an avalanche that buried all 300 residents of Langtang village. Chinese and Nepalese authorities are now warning that a debris-dammed lake at the confluence of two rivers could burst in the coming days, potentially releasing more than two million cubic metres of water into the already devastated valley.

Nepal's government — led by 36-year-old Prime Minister Balendra Shah, a former rapper who took office after mass youth protests — has announced a three-year disaster recovery plan. Officials estimate it will be 2029 at the earliest before full infrastructure, from schools and hospitals to bridges and power, is restored. With 38 schools damaged or destroyed, 10,000 children now have no classrooms.

What Comes Next for the School

For Dawadi, the immediate priority is building temporary learning centres so his Year 10 and Year 12 students can sit their exams. Then he needs to find a safe location for a new school.

He looks across the swirling river to the bodhi tree where his students sheltered as they watched their old school disappear. "That would be a good place," he says.
author: Diaspora Desk
